Lessons.Title: Match and Draw Arrays
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: connect drawings of equal groups with rectangular arrays and draw complete arrays using all original objects. This independently authored Grade 3 U01 L17 teaching follows the 2021 first-edition source skill; publisher images and card sets are not copied.

Warm-up (10 minutes), Which One Doesn't Belong: the original four arrangements A, B, C each contain 15 dots, while D contains 16. Their geometries, not just quantities, are pedagogically important: a student may justify different choices by differences in arrangement. The source notes that B has equal-length rows but an incomplete column and is not a rectangular array. The teacher shows the original images and reviews multiple explanations. Do not mark D as the only correct choice.

Activity 1 (20 minutes), Card Sort: Arrays. Students work in groups of 2 or 4 using original instructor-prepared cards that pair drawings of equal groups with arrays. For a valid match, the group size in the drawing appears in a row OR column of the array. They write one justification, discuss it with peers using MLR1 Stronger and Clearer Each Time, then revise their explanation. This is teacher-observed reasoning; the original blackline deck has not been included in Edulytics and a generic array question is not a substitute for the matching activity.

Activity 2 (15 minutes), Draw Arrays. The first source representation contains four groups of three dots (12 total); learners draw at least one rectangular array using all twelve, for example three rows of four. The second source diagram has sixteen dots; they draw multiple arrays using all sixteen, for example four by four and two by eight. The required products are drawn geometric constructions plus explanations, not just 12 or 16. Original visual geometry/figure rights must be checked separately; Edulytics offers only independent dot-grid examples.

Lesson synthesis (10 minutes): compare matched grouping models, justify constant row and column lengths, and explain how every dot is retained during rearrangement. Teacher assesses source drawing accuracy and spoken reasoning. Cool-down (5 minutes): the original publisher item Draw and Describe is gated; Edulytics instead authors a separate skill-equivalent task to draw two rectangular arrays of sixteen counters and explain them. No student receives automatic academic credit for entering an integer.

KeyConcepts.Title: Valid rectangular array
KeyConcepts.Definition: Objects arranged in complete rows and columns.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Every row and column must have an equal, consistent number of dots; no unfinished edge or missing row.
KeyConcepts.Example: Three complete rows of four form an array of twelve.

KeyConcepts.Title: Array-to-equal-group correspondence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Groups drawn separately can be rearranged into equal rows or columns.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Preserve the count and the size of each equal group, even if rows and columns exchange roles.
KeyConcepts.Example: Four original groups of three can be reorganized into a 4-by-3 array.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare and critique
KeyConcepts.Definition: A picture may fail an array criterion even when its rows appear equal.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check columns too and give an evidence-based explanation; more than one warm-up response may be defensible.
KeyConcepts.Example: A column with fewer dots than the others breaks rectangular completeness.

KeyConcepts.Title: Teacher-evaluated work
KeyConcepts.Definition: The original tasks require drawings, card matching, revision and oral explanation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not equate a numeric total with successful completion of the source tasks.
KeyConcepts.Example: Writing '16' alone does not demonstrate two complete sixteen-dot arrays.

WorkedExamples.Title: Discuss multiple warm-up choices
WorkedExamples.Question: Four original layouts contain 15, 15, 15 and 16 dots. Is the fourth always the only one that does not belong?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare total count AND row/column geometry; avoid imposing one correct response.
Steps: Inspect each original layout, checking complete rows and columns.
Explain a distinguishing property such as total or incomplete column.
Listen for another defensible geometric explanation.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Several explanations may be valid; the publisher's actual geometry determines which arguments are supported.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher-only source image and reasoning review.

WorkedExamples.Title: Twelve-dot array from groups of three
WorkedExamples.Question: Make a rectangular array using four groups of three dots.
WorkedExamples.Method: Keep all twelve dots while aligning equal rows.
Steps: Count four groups with three each, total twelve.
Choose four rows of three or three rows of four.
Draw a rectangular grid with no gaps or extra dots.
Explain how the group size remains visible.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A complete 4-by-3 or 3-by-4 grid of twelve dots.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the student's original construction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Sixteen-dot array variants
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw more than one array containing exactly sixteen dots.
WorkedExamples.Method: Preserve the total and regular row lengths.
Steps: Place sixteen counters into four rows of four.
Rearrange sixteen into two rows of eight.
Check all rows and columns for equal counts.
Explain why both are correct arrays using all sixteen.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Examples include 4-by-4 and 2-by-8, with suitable group explanations.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming every layout with equal row lengths is a full array.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Some original warm-up layouts have incomplete columns.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating the warm-up as a single-answer numeric multiple choice.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Which One Doesn't Belong permits competing arguments supported by visual attributes.
The source explicitly asks for matched cards, drawn arrays and peer explanations.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Review the geometric artifact and justification, not just the total.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Copying unseen source card arrangements into a supposed matched answer key.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original blackline master may include visually important details that have not been inspected.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep source cards teacher-led until each original is verified.

SummaryPoints: 2021 warm-up: three 15-dot arrangements and one 16-dot arrangement; multiple justified answers permitted.
Activity 1: source card sort with group-preserving row/column matches and peer-feedback revision.
Activity 2: draw a complete rectangular arrangement of the original four groups of three, then more than one sixteen-dot array.
Both source drawing tasks require all dots and explanation; a numeric product alone cannot pass.
Student explanations, drawings and original-source card matching remain teacher-assessed.
Edulytics illustrations, independent Practice and Cool-down are not publisher image copies.
Original visual pixels, blackline cards, source task PDF and effective published Rich V2 are not yet fully verified.
All new Stage C tests, CI, Stage D, final approval, merge and deployment remain unperformed.
